definition: Incite means to stir others up toward violent or unlawful action.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word incite. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know incite should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Recruiters moved from table to table in the tavern, inciting men who an hour before had wanted nothing but their supper.
Urge is open, lawful pressure, nowhere near incite — a coach urges the runner on, and nobody calls a constable.

Egging someone on goes further than urging — the pusher wants the stunt for the spectacle of it; incite claims the most: the push aims at something unlawful, and the law counts the pusher among the guilty.

To stir up is the plain kitchen phrase for setting people or feelings in motion — trouble implied, law optional; you can stir up gossip, dust, or a whole town. Incite is the statute's word: the crowd must be pushed toward something violent or unlawful, nothing less.

To whip up is to work a crowd's feeling to a froth — excitement, fury, panic — and the phrase stops at the feeling. Incite goes the further step: the stirred crowd is pointed at a violent or unlawful act, and the pointing itself is what the law punishes.

The rumor of a surprise guest excited the whole arena a full hour before the lights went down.
Incite means to stir others up toward violent or unlawful action.
Chroniclers of the tax revolt give preacher Amos Kale a careful sentence of his own.
For a year his sermons called the land tax wicked — hot words, and only words.
Then, on the last Sunday of Lent, he ended by naming the hour the assessor's cart would reach the ford, and by Monday the cart was in the river.
The revolt had found its first act, and Kale, who never left his pulpit, had incited it — supplying its time and place.
Incite is the exact word for that last sermon, because to incite is to stir others up toward violent or unlawful action — the inciter supplies the heat and the direction, and other hands do the rest.
A year of preaching had merely made the tax hateful.
One sentence told hatred where to stand and when.

Incite lives in criminal statutes and referees' reports, and it needs three things: a pusher, a crowd, and an unlawful or violent aim.
Instigate, its unit-mate, works one quarrel and often works it in whispers; incite is loud and aimed.
The act built to draw rage is a provocation, and language built for the purpose is incendiary.

At the trial, nobody disputed what the foreman had said at the gates — only what the words were for.
The company's lawyers read the speech as a set of orders: the evening shift should follow him to the substation and pull the switches, whatever the watchmen did.
The defense read the same lines as anger and nothing more, the ordinary heat of a man cheated on wages.
The judge put the question narrowly: a man may denounce, may protest, may even frighten — but to incite is to push others toward breaking the law, and that is where speech stops being protected.
The jury weighed one sentence for two days: 'Go and take back what the company stole.'
